title: Halal living
description: Practical beginner guidance for food, social meals, money, entertainment, and everyday choices.

sections.heading: Start with clear food basics
sections.content:
The early food priorities are simple: avoid pork and alcohol, choose halal meat when you can get it, and work through the unclear ingredients over time. You do not need to become an ingredient expert overnight.

Vegetarian meals, seafood, eggs, dairy, beans, rice, and plain home cooking make the first few months much easier.

sections.heading: Restaurants and social meals
sections.content:
Plan ahead where you can. Check menus, pick the clearer options, and tell hosts what you need in one sentence. You can say: **I eat halal now, so I avoid pork and alcohol. I am happy to bring something if that helps.**

Try not to turn every meal into a debate. Quiet consistency teaches people more than a long explanation does.

sections.heading: Everyday situations
sections.content: New Muslims often worry about the same handful of everyday questions. The short answers below give the mainstream view, where scholars differ, and what can wait while you settle into prayer and the basics. Each one is general guidance, so ask a teacher you trust about your own situation.

sections.heading: Shaking hands
sections.content:
Most scholars of the four schools say a man and a woman who are not close family should not shake hands. They rely on reports such as Aisha's statement that the Prophet never touched a woman's hand when taking the pledge (Sahih Muslim 1866b). An AMJA scholar advises explaining that you avoid it out of respect, not dislike, and that if you are caught in a moment you could not avoid, you simply ask Allah's forgiveness.

Egypt's Dar al-Ifta calls this a disputed question. It says a Muslim may follow the scholars who allow a handshake without desire, especially in non-Muslim countries, to avoid embarrassing others. Because it is a real difference of opinion, nobody should shame you for either choice.

A friendly script if you choose not to shake hands: put your hand on your heart, smile, and say, "I don't shake hands for religious reasons, but it's really nice to meet you."

**What can wait:** you do not need to settle this before your next day at work. Ask your local imam which view to follow.

sections.heading: Tattoos from before Islam
sections.content:
AMJA scholars explain that what you did before Islam is forgiven, and that you do not need to remove a tattoo if removal would be costly or harmful. You do not have to cover tattoos when you pray. You may cover them in the masjid if you like, without being hard on yourself, and uncovering them in hot weather is fine. The Prophet told a new Muslim, "You became Muslim with all those good deeds" (Sahih al-Bukhari 1436). The same AMJA answer says getting new tattoos is not permitted.

**What can wait:** any decision about removal. There is nothing urgent here.

sections.heading: Dogs
sections.content:
An AMJA answer written for converts and a SeekersGuidance answer from the Hanafi school both discourage keeping a dog as an indoor pet, while allowing working dogs such as guard dogs, kept outside. The AMJA answer advises keeping a guard dog outside or finding it a new home. Some scholars, notably in the Maliki school, are known for a more lenient view, so ask a teacher about that too.

**What can wait:** please do not make a sudden decision that hurts your family or the animal. Talk to a scholar first, especially if the dog belongs to other family members, is a service dog, or lives in a shared home.

sections.heading: Music
sections.content:
Muslims have disagreed about music for centuries. A SeekersGuidance answer explains that most scholars of the four schools restrict musical instruments, apart from the duff (a hand drum), which the Hanafi school and others allow, while singing with clean words is fine. A report in Sahih al-Bukhari (5590) is often cited for this view, and its chain is itself discussed by scholars. Some scholars, such as Imam al-Ghazali, and today Egypt's Dar al-Ifta, allow music whose words and setting are clean. Everyone agrees that lyrics promoting sin are a problem. An AMJA scholar adds that hearing music you did not choose, such as in a shop, is not held against you.

**What can wait:** you do not need to make a sudden change on day one. Focus on prayer and the basics first, then learn about this with a teacher you trust.

sections.heading: Free time: screens, games, photos and nights out
sections.content:
Free time is part of a Muslim life, and you do not need to delete every game or photo in a panic.

For films and streaming, a SeekersGuidance answer by Shaykh Irshaad Sedick, checked by Shaykh Faraz Rabbani, says subscribing to a streaming service is not direct help in sin. Watching lawful content within reasonable limits is fine, unless it pulls you away from your duties. A simple test: skip what you would be uncomfortable watching next to your teacher.

Video games raise the same two questions: what the game shows, and how much time it takes. A Shafi'i teacher on SeekersGuidance calls unnecessary online activity with the opposite sex, such as gaming together, undoubtedly inappropriate. Turning off voice chat with strangers is an easy first step.

On photos, contemporary scholars differ. A SeekersGuidance answer by Shaykh Dr. Muhammad Abu Bakr Badhib reports that some scholars permit photography, while others say corrupting images are forbidden and other photos are better avoided, with educational and medical images allowed. An AMJA fatwa by Dr. Ibrahim Dremali is stricter and prohibits camera photos except for necessity, need or a recognised interest. Another AMJA fatwa, by Dr. Salah Al-Sawy, says posting personal photos publicly, especially of women, is not permissible. Ask your teacher which view to follow. Whatever you decide, check your privacy settings before you post about your conversion, especially if your family does not know yet.

When a night out centres on drinking, suggest another plan, such as dinner and a movie. "No thanks, I don't drink" is a complete answer. Dancing and concerts are not covered here yet, so ask a teacher, and see the music section above.

Pictures at home are a related question. Hadiths in Sahih al-Bukhari say angels do not enter a house with a picture of a living creature (3225) and warn picture-makers of the severest punishment (5950). Scholars differ on how far these reach, for example whether they include photographs, as described above. Before you take down family photos in a way that would hurt relatives, ask a teacher, and do it gently.

sections.heading: Gambling, lotteries and office pools
sections.content:
The Quran lists gambling with intoxicants as something to avoid (5:90). That includes lottery tickets, casino games, sports betting and paid office pools where everyone puts in money and one person wins. Free prize draws are a separate question: an AMJA scholar, Dr. Hatem al-Haj, says a draw with no payment or purchase condition is not gambling, if it is as described.

If a coworker invites you into a pool, a light answer works: "I'll sit this one out, but good luck!"

**What can wait:** the finer cases, such as store promotions, which you can ask a teacher about later.

sections.heading: Smoking and vaping
sections.content:
A SeekersGuidance answer summarises the views: many contemporary scholars consider smoking forbidden or strongly disliked because of its proven harm, and others call it disliked. Cannabis takes the ruling of alcohol because it intoxicates. The answer does not address vaping, so ask a teacher about it.

**What can wait:** quitting nicotine is hard, and Islam values steady progress. Your doctor can help you plan it, and you can make it part of your new start without shame.

sections.heading: Halal labels and certifiers in Canada
sections.content:
In Canada, a food label, package or advertisement that says or suggests **halal**, including through Arabic letters or symbols, must also show the name of the person or organisation that certified it. This is a federal labelling rule enforced by the Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA). The CFIA does not decide what counts as halal or approve certifiers.

So the next step is yours: look for the certifier's name, then ask your local masjid which certifiers it trusts. Names you will see include the Halal Monitoring Authority (HMA) and ISNA Canada Halal. Their standards are not identical, for example on machine slaughter and stunning, and HMA's own FAQ notes that many scholars approve machine-slaughtered chicken that HMA does not. If a shop or restaurant says halal with no certifier shown, HMA suggests asking to see the certificate and calling the certifier. We do not recommend one certifier over another.

**What can wait:** becoming an ingredient expert. Start with the clear choices and learn the rest over time.

sections.heading: Winter clothing and wudu in the cold
sections.content:
Modest clothing and a Canadian winter can work together. Long coats, layers, scarves and hats are all modest, and you do not need to buy a new wardrobe. We did not find a scholarly source written about winter clothing, so these practical points are our own suggestions, not rulings.

For wudu in the cold, a SeekersGuidance answer from the Shafi'i school suggests keeping warm water ready, warming the bathroom, drying with a towel if you need to, and washing each limb once instead of three times. It also mentions leather socks (khuffs) that you wipe over instead of washing your feet. Many scholars allow wiping over suitable socks if you put them on after a full wudu, for one day and night at home or three when travelling. The schools differ on which socks count: the Hanafi school requires thick socks you could walk in.

**What can wait:** the details of wiping over socks. Wash your feet as normal until a teacher has shown you.

sections.heading: Money and work
sections.content:
This section is an introduction only. It is general education, not financial, legal or religious advice for your case.

**Interest (riba):** the Quran permits trade and forbids interest (2:275), and tells believers to give up what remains of interest owed to them (2:278-279). A hadith in Sahih Muslim (1598) says the Prophet cursed the one who takes interest, the one who pays it, the one who records it and the witnesses.

**If you already have loans:** many new Muslims arrive with a mortgage, a car loan, credit cards or student loans. Please do not panic or break contracts overnight. Keep paying what you owe, pay credit cards in full each month so you are not charged interest, avoid new interest-based debt where you can, and ask a qualified scholar and a financial adviser before changing anything.

**Mortgages and Islamic home financing:** many scholars, including SeekersGuidance teachers, say a conventional interest mortgage should be avoided in favour of an Islamic financing option, ideally one checked by a board of qualified scholars. Islamic products differ from a loan in the contract itself, such as who owns the home, who carries the risk and a single known price, even when the monthly cost looks similar, and some providers are structured more carefully than others. One SeekersGuidance answer says moving an existing conventional mortgage to a Shari'ah-compliant option is strongly advised or even required. Egypt's Dar al-Ifta takes a different view and allows a bank home loan as a form of sale (murabaha). In Budget 2024 the federal government said halal mortgage products exist in Canada and that it was exploring tax and regulatory changes to widen access. We do not name or recommend providers.

**Student loans:** since 1 April 2023 the federal Canada Student Loan charges no interest. The Government of Canada made this permanent for Canada Student Loans and Canada Apprentice Loans, but interest that built up before that date is still owed. Quebec, the Northwest Territories and Nunavut run their own student aid, so this federal change does not cover them.

Your aid may also include a provincial or territorial loan, and each province sets its own terms. Ontario, for example, still charges interest on the Ontario part of an OSAP loan, including during the six-month grace period after you finish school. So do not assume all student aid carries interest, and do not assume none of it does. Read your loan agreement for each part, and ask your financial aid office whether you can take less of any part that charges interest.

One SeekersGuidance answer says taking an interest-bearing student loan is not permitted, and suggests saving first, studying part time or borrowing interest-free from family or friends. Scholars differ on loans with any interest element, and a loan that mixes an interest-free part with an interest-bearing part is a question for a qualified scholar.

**Interest paid to you:** if your bank account pays interest, AMJA fatwa 4170 (Dr. Salah al-Sawy, 2012) says to give it away to causes that benefit the public. It may go to relatives in need, but not to your parents, because supporting them is already your duty. The same answer advises moving your savings to an Islamic option where you can. A no-interest account avoids the question.

**Workplace pensions and investing:** the Canada Revenue Agency says a TFSA can hold cash, stocks, bonds, mutual funds and ETFs. The account is a set of tax rules. What you hold inside it is the religious question. AMJA fatwa 1774 (Dr. Hatem al-Haj, 2006, written for a US 401(k)) says joining an employer retirement plan is permissible, especially when your employer matches your contributions. It says to choose Islamic funds first, then screened stock funds, and to avoid bonds. AMJA fatwa 2066 (Dr. Main Khalid al-Qudah, 2006) says investing through a screened fund is allowed if you give away the share of profit that came from prohibited income, which is called purification. Scholars differ on screening rules and on how much to give away. Check the fund list in your workplace plan before you turn down an employer match.

**CPP and QPP:** the Government of Canada says anyone over 18 who works in Canada outside Quebec and earns more than $3,500 a year must pay into the Canada Pension Plan. Quebec has its own plan (QPP). AMJA's 2005 resolution on insurance treats government social insurance as acceptable. If you still have questions about it, ask a scholar.

**Work and zakat:** zakat, investments and complicated employment questions belong with qualified scholars or professionals who understand your local context.

Before you sign, refinance or cancel anything, speak with a qualified scholar and a licensed financial adviser.

sections.heading: Avoid obsessiveness
sections.content: Halal living is supposed to bring obedience and peace. If it is bringing panic instead, something has gone off track. When you find yourself checking labels over and over, avoiding ordinary life, or trapped by doubts, ask a qualified teacher for a simple beginner standard to work from.
